title: The Softmax Bottleneck Does Not Limit the Probabilities of the Most Likely Tokens
claim: Even random projection matrices match trained ones in representing top-m probabilities, far beyond what the theoretical lower bound guarantees.
layout: 5 line-plot panels, one wide on top, 2x2 grid below; shared purple bound
description: A set of five line plots, each with m on the x-axis and the fraction of successful trials (0 to 1) on the y-axis. One wide GPT2 panel sits on top. Below it is a 2x2 grid for T5-Large, GPT2-XL, TinyLlama and Llama2. Each panel has a solid blue curve for the trained matrix and a dotted blue curve for a random matrix of the same size. Both stay at 1 and then drop sharply to 0 at nearly the same m. A dotted purple lower-bound curve falls to 0 much earlier, well to the left. The GPT2 panel also has orange curves for prescribed top-m probabilities, which drop earlier. Square markers mark the data points. Legends are in the lower left of each panel. The eye goes first to the steep sigmoid drop-offs and the gap between the purple and blue curves.
caption: Top: Top-m probability for the GPT-2 and random GPT2-sized (50257 × 768) output projection matrices. Curves show the fraction of times that the matrix satisfied desired constraints for m randomly chosen tokens as m increases. We show our lower bound for a random matrix (4) in dotted purple, along with linear-programming simulations for a random matrix (dotted blue) and the trained GPT-2 (solid blue) matrix. Also in this panel, we show LP simulations with prescribed top-m probabilities (random matrices in dotted red and the trained GPT-2 matrix in solid red). Other: Similarly, for T5-Large, GPT-XL, TinyLlama, and Llama2 and corresponding random matrices of the same size TinyLlama-sized, we show our lower bound (4) in dotted purple along with linear program simulations for random matrices (dotted blue) and the trained matrix (solid blue).
abstract: In many popular transformer architectures, an output projection matrix linearly maps lower-dimensional embeddings into a higher-dimensional space of logits. It has been shown that this leads to a softmax bottleneck that prevents the production of arbitrary probability distributions. It has been argued that this limits large language models (LLMs) in their ability to express next token probabilities that perfectly align with the statistics of natural language. We focus on the ability of such models to produce accurate probabilities for just the top-$m$ tokens. We provide theoretical bounds that show that even a randomly initialized projection matrix can successfully do this for rather large values of $m$, supported by empirical results on both random and trained matrices. This raises questions about whether the softmax bottleneck significantly limits the capabilities of LLMs. We also derive bounds on the maximum number of probabilities that any trained output projection matrix can specify.
